a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.prompt: Every GPT-style model is trained only to predict the next token. Why is that enough to define a probability for a whole document?
options: The chain rule assumes each token depends only on the one before it, which is close enough for text.
The factorization is exact only when tokens are independent, which long documents approximately are.
Next-token prediction approximates the joint, and a separate document-level model corrects the remaining error.
The chain rule $P(w_{1:n})=\prod_t P(w_t\mid w_{<t})$ is exact, so the conditionals fix the joint probability.
a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.explanation: The chain rule of probability holds for any distribution, with no independence or Markov assumption: each factor conditions on the entire prefix. A model of every next-token conditional is therefore a complete model of sequences, and sampling token by token generates from it.

a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.prompt: A model gives these conditional probabilities: $P(\text{The})=0.2$, $P(\text{flask}\mid\text{The})=0.05$, $P(\text{cracked}\mid\text{The flask})=0.3$, $P(\text{.}\mid\text{The flask cracked})=0.5$. What is $\log_2 P$ of the four-token sentence? Give the answer in bits (a negative number).
a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.explanation: $P=0.2\times0.05\times0.3\times0.5=1.5\times10^{-3}$, so $\log_2P=\log_2 0.2+\log_2 0.05+\log_2 0.3+\log_2 0.5\approx-9.38$ bits. The sum of per-token log-probabilities gives the same number without ever forming the tiny product.

a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.prompt: Why do language-model codes add log-probabilities instead of multiplying the raw token probabilities?
options: A long text's probability (say $10^{-2000}$) underflows to zero in floating point; its log is a modest number.
Multiplication is much slower than addition on GPUs, and the speed-up is the main reason for working in log space.
Log-probabilities are always positive, which avoids sign errors when many factors are combined together.
Raw probabilities are not normalized over the vocabulary, while their logarithms automatically are.
a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.explanation: Each factor is below 1, so the product shrinks exponentially with length and falls below the smallest representable double (about $10^{-308}$) after a few hundred tokens. Logs turn the product into a sum of moderate negative numbers that floating point handles easily.

a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.prompt: Explain in your own words why a model that only ever predicts the next token can still assign a probability to, and generate, whole documents.
a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the chain rule writes any sequence probability exactly as a product of next-token conditionals, each conditioned on the full prefix; (2) so learning all conditionals is learning the joint distribution, with no independence assumption; (3) generation samples one token, appends it and repeats, which samples from that joint; (4) in practice the product is evaluated as a sum of log-probabilities.
a4-l001-language-modeling-problem.modelAnswer: By the chain rule, $P(w_{1:n})=\prod_t P(w_t\mid w_{<t})$ exactly, with each factor seeing the whole prefix. A model of every next-token conditional is therefore a model of whole sequences: its log-probability for a document is the sum of per-token log-probabilities, and sampling a token, appending it and repeating draws documents from that same distribution.

a4-l002-ngrams-markov.prompt: In a lab-notebook corpus the word 'reaction' occurs 20 times, and 6 of those are followed by 'mixture'. The vocabulary has $V=50$ words. What is the add-one (Laplace) smoothed bigram probability $P(\text{mixture}\mid\text{reaction})$? Give a decimal.
a4-l002-ngrams-markov.explanation: $(6+1)/(20+50)=0.10$, down from the unsmoothed $6/20=0.30$. Adding one to every count moves probability mass to the many unseen bigrams, and with a small context count and large $V$ that shift is large.

a4-l002-ngrams-markov.prompt: A trigram model reads 'The flask that the student heated ___'. What does it use to predict the blank?
options: The whole sentence, weighted toward the most recent words.
The subject 'The flask', since verbs agree with subjects.
Only the two preceding words, 'student heated'.
An average of every trigram that occurs in the sentence.
a4-l002-ngrams-markov.explanation: The Markov assumption truncates the context to the previous $n-1$ words. Anything earlier, including the subject that controls agreement and meaning, is invisible to the model.

a4-l002-ngrams-markov.prompt: Why do count-based 5-gram models generalize poorly even when trained on billions of words?
options: Five words give too little context to capture grammar, so longer windows would solve the problem.
Most 5-word sequences in new text never occurred in training, so their counts are zero or tiny.
Counting 5-grams is computationally impossible, so the tables are always truncated at random.
Higher-order n-gram probabilities no longer sum to one, so the model is not a valid distribution.
a4-l002-ngrams-markov.explanation: The number of possible n-grams grows as $V^n$, so counts become hopelessly sparse as $n$ grows: a novel sentence is mostly made of 5-grams never seen before. Counts also treat every word as an unrelated symbol, so evidence about one word never transfers to a similar one. That is the opening for neural models.

a4-l002-ngrams-markov.prompt: Explain why an n-gram model needs smoothing, and why the sparsity problem gets worse as $n$ grows, in a way that motivates neural language models.
a4-l002-ngrams-markov.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) maximum-likelihood counts give zero probability to any unseen n-gram, so a single unseen n-gram makes a whole test sentence impossible (infinite loss); (2) smoothing such as add-one reserves some mass for unseen events; (3) the number of possible n-grams grows exponentially with n, so longer contexts are seen too rarely to estimate; (4) counts cannot share evidence between similar words, which learned embeddings in neural models can.
a4-l002-ngrams-markov.modelAnswer: Raw counts assign zero probability to anything not seen in training, so one unseen bigram makes a perfectly good sentence 'impossible'; smoothing reserves a little mass for unseen events. Longer contexts help in principle, but the number of possible n-grams grows like $V^n$, so most long contexts are never seen at all. Counts treat 'benzene' and 'toluene' as unrelated symbols, so nothing learned about one helps the other; neural models fix this by mapping words to shared vectors.

a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.prompt: A next-token distribution spreads equally over 8 tokens, so $H=3$ bits. A system with 8 equally likely microstates has Gibbs entropy $S=-k_B\sum p_i\ln p_i$. How are the two related?
options: $S=3\,k_B$, because a bit and $k_B$ are the same unit of entropy.
$S=8\,k_B$, because Gibbs entropy simply counts the number of microstates directly.
They are unrelated, since information entropy has no physical units.
$S=k_B\ln 8=3\,k_B\ln 2$: the same sum, with each bit worth $k_B\ln 2$.
a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.explanation: Both are $-\sum p\log p$ over a probability distribution; they differ only in the log base and the constant. Converting bits to thermodynamic units multiplies by $k_B\ln 2$, so 3 bits corresponds to $3k_B\ln 2=k_B\ln 8$, the Boltzmann $k_B\ln W$ for $W=8$.

a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.prompt: Why does minimizing the average cross-entropy loss on a training corpus amount to maximum-likelihood estimation?
options: Cross-entropy equals the KL divergence exactly, and KL is zero only when the model reproduces the training data.
The loss is minus the mean log-probability the model gives the observed tokens, so lowering it raises their likelihood.
Cross-entropy only penalizes the most probable token, which is the same as choosing the mode of the data.
Maximum likelihood needs a uniform prior over the parameters, and the cross-entropy loss supplies that prior automatically.
a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.explanation: The empirical cross-entropy $-\frac1N\sum_t\log q(w_t\mid w_{<t})$ is $-\frac1N\log$ of the likelihood of the data, so its minimum is the maximum-likelihood fit. Equivalently $H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)$, and since $H(p)$ is fixed, minimizing cross-entropy minimizes the KL divergence from the data distribution.

a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.prompt: The true next-token distribution over two tokens is $p=(0.5,\,0.5)$ and a model predicts $q=(0.25,\,0.75)$. What is $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)$? Give the answer in bits.
a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.explanation: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.5\log_2\frac{0.5}{0.25}+0.5\log_2\frac{0.5}{0.75}=0.5-0.292=0.208$ bits. The cross-entropy is $H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}=1.208$ bits: the model pays about 0.21 extra bits per token for being wrong.

a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.prompt: A language model's average loss on held-out text is 3 bits per token. Convert this to perplexity and explain what the number means.
a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) perplexity $=2^{H}=2^3=8$ (or $e^{H}$ if the loss is in nats); (2) interpretation as an effective branching factor: the model is as uncertain as if choosing uniformly among about 8 tokens at each step; (3) lower perplexity means the model is less surprised by real text, with 1 as the floor for perfect prediction.
a4-l003-entropy-cross-entropy.modelAnswer: Perplexity is $2^{3}=8$. The model is, on average, as uncertain as if it had to pick uniformly among 8 equally likely tokens at every step, even though the real vocabulary has tens of thousands of entries. A perfect predictor would have perplexity 1; the lower the number, the fewer effective choices the model is torn between.

a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.prompt: Run byte-pair encoding on a corpus whose words (with counts) are: hug ×10, pug ×5, pun ×12, bun ×4, hugs ×5. Starting from single characters, which two merges are learned first?
options: p+u → pu (17), then u+n → un (16).
u+n → un (16), then u+g → ug (20).
u+g → ug (20), then u+n → un (16).
h+u → hu (15), then hu+g → hug (15).
a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.explanation: Count adjacent pairs weighted by word frequency: u g occurs in hug, pug and hugs ($10+5+5=20$), p u in pug and pun (17), u n in pun and bun (16), h u in hug and hugs (15). Merge u g first; after that p u only occurs in pun (12), so u n (16) is the next most frequent pair. BPE always merges the currently most frequent pair.

a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.prompt: Why do modern LLMs use byte-level subword vocabularies rather than whole words or single characters?
options: Subwords keep sequences short, and a byte base alphabet means no input character is ever out of vocabulary.
Word vocabularies are too small to cover chemistry terms, while character vocabularies are far too large.
Character-level models cannot learn spelling at all, while subword models store each spelling exactly.
Attention can only handle 256 distinct symbols at once, so the whole vocabulary must be built up from raw bytes.
a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.explanation: Words give short sequences but a huge vocabulary with unknown words; characters never fail but make sequences long and expensive under $O(n^2)$ attention. Subwords sit in between, and starting BPE from the 256 byte values guarantees any string, in any script or notation, can be encoded.

a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.prompt: A general-purpose BPE tokenizer is applied to numbers like 12345 and to SMILES strings like CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O. Explain what artifacts to expect and why they hurt arithmetic and chemistry tasks.
a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) merges were learned mostly on ordinary text, so digits group irregularly (e.g. 123|45) and the same number can split differently in different contexts, which hides place value; (2) SMILES fragment at chemically meaningless points: ring-closure digits, bonds, branches and bracket atoms such as [C@@H] may merge with neighbours differently each time, so matching ring-opening and ring-closing digits or a stereocentre look unrelated to the model; (3) this makes digit-wise arithmetic and structure-level reasoning harder and lengthens sequences.
a4-l004-tokenization-bpe.modelAnswer: Merges are learned from mostly English text, so digit strings break into irregular chunks (12345 might become 123|45 here and 1|2345 elsewhere) and the model never sees a consistent place-value structure, which hurts carrying and comparison. SMILES split at arbitrary points: the '1' that opens a benzene ring might fuse with 'c' as 'c1' while the closing '1' joins a different token, and bracket atoms like [C@@H] fragment. Chemically meaningful units are hidden, so the model struggles to track rings, branches and stereochemistry.

a4-l005-embeddings.prompt: A token is represented as a one-hot vector $e_i$ and multiplied by the embedding matrix $E$ (one row per token). What does the product do?
options: It averages all rows of $E$, weighted by how often each token occurs.
It projects the token onto the principal components of the vocabulary.
It picks out row $i$ of $E$: a table lookup of learned vectors.
It returns the index $i$ as a scalar that the network then rescales.
a4-l005-embeddings.explanation: A one-hot vector has a single 1, so $E^{\top}e_i$ selects one row. Implementations skip the multiplication and index the table directly; the rows are ordinary parameters learned by gradient descent.

a4-l005-embeddings.prompt: Two word vectors are $u=(1,2,2)$ and $v=(2,1,2)$. What is their cosine similarity? Give a decimal.
a4-l005-embeddings.explanation: $u\cdot v=2+2+4=8$ and $\|u\|=\|v\|=3$, so $\cos\theta=8/9\approx0.889$. Cosine ignores vector length and measures only direction, which is why it is the standard similarity for embeddings.

a4-l005-embeddings.prompt: Word2vec vectors satisfy king − man + woman ≈ queen. Which statement is a genuine limitation of such embeddings?
options: One vector per word blends all its senses, so 'bond' (chemical or financial) gets one compromise.
The analogy holds exactly, because training forces every relation to be a fixed linear offset.
Each dimension stores one named concept, such as gender, so other kinds of relation cannot be encoded.
The vectors are hand-designed by linguists, so they only contain relations someone chose to add.
a4-l005-embeddings.explanation: Static embeddings give each word type a single vector, so polysemous words are averaged across senses. Analogies are approximate (they hold only after excluding the input words from the search), are weaker for rare words, and reflect biases in the training text. Individual dimensions have no assigned meaning.

a4-l005-embeddings.prompt: Explain the distributional hypothesis and why it makes words that appear in similar contexts end up with similar embedding vectors.
a4-l005-embeddings.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the hypothesis that a word's meaning is reflected in the contexts it occurs in ('you shall know a word by the company it keeps'); (2) word2vec-style training adjusts vectors so a word predicts (or is predicted by) its context words; (3) words with similar contexts receive similar gradient updates and are pulled toward the same context vectors, so their own vectors become close (high cosine similarity).
a4-l005-embeddings.modelAnswer: The distributional hypothesis says words used in similar contexts have similar meanings. Word2vec trains each word's vector to predict its neighbouring words. 'Ethanol' and 'methanol' appear next to the same words (solvent, distil, flammable), so the training signal pushes their vectors toward the same context vectors, and they end up pointing in similar directions.

a4-l006-softmax-temperature.prompt: Adding 5 to every logit before the softmax does what to the output probabilities?
options: It sharpens them, because larger logits act like a lower temperature.
Nothing: the shift cancels between numerator and normalizer, like moving the zero of energy.
It flattens them, because the relative gaps between the logits shrink.
It raises every probability, so they no longer sum to one and must be renormalized afterwards.
a4-l006-softmax-temperature.explanation: $e^{z_i+c}/\sum_j e^{z_j+c}=e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$. In Boltzmann terms, shifting every energy by the same amount changes $Z$ by a constant factor and leaves populations unchanged. Only differences between logits (and the temperature) matter.

a4-l006-softmax-temperature.prompt: Logits for three tokens are $(2,\,1,\,0)$. Sampling at temperature $T=0.5$, what probability does the softmax give the first token? Give a decimal.
a4-l006-softmax-temperature.explanation: Dividing by $T=0.5$ gives $(4,2,0)$, so $p_1=e^4/(e^4+e^2+e^0)=54.6/63.0\approx0.867$, compared with 0.665 at $T=1$. Halving the temperature doubles every energy gap, so the lowest-energy (highest-logit) state dominates more.

a4-l006-softmax-temperature.prompt: For logits $(2,1,0)$, how does the entropy of the softmax output change as $T$ goes from 0.1 to 1 to 10?
options: It falls, because higher temperature concentrates probability onto the top token.
It stays at $\log_2 3$ bits, because the number of available options never changes.
It peaks near $T=1$ and then falls at high $T$, where the largest logit comes to dominate again.
It rises from near 0 toward $\log_2 3\approx1.58$ bits, as more levels become populated.
a4-l006-softmax-temperature.explanation: At low $T$ almost all probability sits on the top token (the ground state), so entropy is near zero. Raising $T$ populates the higher-'energy' tokens, and as $T\to\infty$ all three become equally likely with entropy $\log_2 3$. Entropy rises monotonically with $T$, just as in a heated multi-level system.

a4-l006-softmax-temperature.prompt: Explain why softmax with temperature is the Boltzmann distribution, and predict what happens to the output as $T\to0$ and as $T\to\infty$.
a4-l006-softmax-temperature.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) matching $p_i\propto e^{z_i/T}$ with $p_i\propto e^{-E_i/k_BT}$, so logits play the role of negative energies and the normalizer is the partition function $Z$; (2) $T\to0$: all probability on the highest logit (ground state only), i.e. greedy argmax; (3) $T\to\infty$: uniform over all tokens, like a system where every level is equally populated.
a4-l006-softmax-temperature.modelAnswer: Softmax $p_i=e^{z_i/T}/\sum_j e^{z_j/T}$ is the Boltzmann form $e^{-E_i/k_BT}/Z$ with $E_i=-z_i$: a high logit is a low-energy state and the denominator is the partition function. As $T\to0$ only the ground state (top logit) is occupied, which is greedy decoding. As $T\to\infty$ the energy differences stop mattering and every token becomes equally likely.

a4-l007-neural-language-models.prompt: A fixed-window neural language model has vocabulary $V=10{,}000$, embedding width $d=64$, a context of $k=3$ previous tokens, and one hidden layer of 256 units feeding a softmax over the vocabulary. Ignoring biases, how many parameters does it have?
a4-l007-neural-language-models.explanation: Embedding table $Vd=640{,}000$; hidden layer $(kd)\times256=49{,}152$; output layer $256\times V=2{,}560{,}000$; total 3,249,152. The vocabulary-sized output layer dominates, a pattern that persists in larger models' embedding and unembedding matrices.

a4-l007-neural-language-models.prompt: In a fixed-window feed-forward language model, what happens to the $k$ previous tokens before the hidden layer?
options: Each is mapped to its embedding vector and the $k$ vectors are concatenated.
Their one-hot vectors are summed, so the order of the words does not matter.
They are counted, and the counts are passed to the hidden layer as features.
Each goes to a separate network, and the outputs are multiplied together.
a4-l007-neural-language-models.explanation: Concatenation keeps the position of each context word, and the shared embedding table maps every word to a dense vector. A hidden layer then mixes them and a softmax gives a distribution over the next token.

a4-l007-neural-language-models.prompt: A count-based trigram model gives 'toluene was distilled' only a smoothed, near-zero probability because that trigram never occurred, while a neural model rates it as plausible. Why?
options: The neural network memorizes every trigram in a table larger than a count model could store.
'Toluene' gets an embedding near 'benzene', so patterns learned for one transfer to the other.
The neural model applies Laplace smoothing internally, giving unseen trigrams a fair probability.
A softmax output can never be exactly zero, and this alone is why the neural model generalizes.
a4-l007-neural-language-models.explanation: Words used in similar contexts receive similar embedding vectors, and the network's output is a smooth function of those vectors. So evidence from 'benzene was distilled' raises the probability of 'toluene was distilled'. A count model treats each word as an unrelated symbol and cannot share evidence.

a4-l007-neural-language-models.prompt: Explain what limitation a fixed-window neural language model still shares with an n-gram model, and what it gains over one.
a4-l007-neural-language-models.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) shared limitation: it conditions only on the previous k tokens (a Markov assumption), so earlier context cannot influence the prediction; (2) gain: dense shared embeddings let it generalize to unseen word combinations by similarity; (3) parameters grow linearly in k rather than exponentially as count tables do.
a4-l007-neural-language-models.modelAnswer: Like an n-gram model, it sees only a fixed window of $k$ previous tokens, so anything earlier is forgotten. What it gains is generalization: words become dense vectors, so similar words share statistics and unseen combinations get sensible probabilities, and the parameter count grows only linearly with $k$ instead of the $V^n$ blow-up of count tables.

a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.prompt: A query has dot products $(1,\,0,\,2)$ with three keys, whose values are $v_1=(1,0)$, $v_2=(0,1)$, $v_3=(1,1)$. Using softmax attention weights (no scaling), what is the first component of the output vector? Give a decimal.
a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.explanation: Softmax of $(1,0,2)$ gives weights $(0.245,\,0.090,\,0.665)$. The output is $\sum_j a_j v_j=(0.245+0.665,\ 0.090+0.665)=(0.910,\,0.755)$, a blend of the values dominated by the best-matching key.

a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.prompt: In self-attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
options: Three separate embedding tables, each looked up for every token.
The token vector itself, used three times without change.
Fixed random projections chosen once and never trained.
Three learned linear maps applied to the same token vectors.
a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.explanation: $Q=XW_Q$, $K=XW_K$, $V=XW_V$ with learned matrices. Each token thus plays three roles: what it is looking for (query), what it advertises (key), and what it hands over if selected (value).

a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.prompt: Every query vector in an attention layer is multiplied by 3. What happens to the attention weights?
options: Nothing changes, because softmax ignores the overall scale of its inputs.
They become more uniform, because large scores saturate the exponential.
They sharpen toward the best-matching key, like cooling a Boltzmann distribution.
The output vector triples in size, but the weights over the keys stay exactly the same.
a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.explanation: Scaling the scores by 3 is the same as dividing the temperature by 3: score gaps grow and the softmax concentrates on the highest score. Softmax ignores additive shifts, not multiplicative scale.

a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.prompt: Explain why attention lets a token use information from any other token in a single layer, and why this is an advantage over a recurrent network.
a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) every query is compared with every key directly, and the output is a weighted sum over all values, so any two positions are connected by a path of length one; (2) a recurrent network must pass information step by step through its hidden state, so distant information is squeezed and degraded over many steps (and gradients vanish); (3) attention also computes all positions in parallel, unlike the sequential RNN.
a4-l008-attention-soft-lookup.modelAnswer: Each token's query is scored against every key and the output mixes all value vectors, so information from token 1 can reach token 500 in one step. An RNN has to carry that information through 499 successive updates of a fixed-size hidden state, where it gets overwritten and its gradient fades. Attention also processes all positions in parallel, which suits GPUs.

a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.prompt: For one head with sequence length $n$, model width $d$ and key width $d_k$, $Q=XW_Q$ with $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$. What is the shape of $QK^{\top}$?
options: $d_k\times d_k$, one score per pair of key features.
$n\times n$, one score for every query–key pair.
$n\times d_k$, the same shape as the query matrix.
$d\times d$, the shape of the projection matrices.
a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.explanation: $Q$ and $K$ are both $n\times d_k$, so $QK^{\top}$ is $n\times n$. After the softmax it multiplies $V$ ($n\times d_v$) to give an $n\times d_v$ output. The $n\times n$ score matrix is where attention's quadratic cost comes from.

a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.prompt: Why are attention scores divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$?
options: Without it the attention weights would not sum to one over the keys in each row.
It rescales every score to unit norm, which the softmax requires of its inputs.
Raw scores have variance $d_k$, so they would grow with width and saturate the softmax.
It offsets the extra parameters in wider heads, keeping the model's total parameter count fixed.
a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.explanation: For random vectors with unit-variance entries, $q\cdot k$ is a sum of $d_k$ products and has variance $d_k$. Large scores act like a very low temperature: the softmax becomes nearly one-hot and its gradients vanish. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance.

a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.prompt: A single attention head processes $n=32{,}768$ tokens and stores its score matrix in 16-bit floats (2 bytes each). How much memory does the score matrix take? Give the answer in GB ($10^9$ bytes).
a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.explanation: $n^2\times2=32768^2\times2\approx2.15\times10^9$ bytes, about 2.1 GB for one head in one layer. Avoiding ever materializing this matrix is the point of tiled kernels such as FlashAttention.

a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.prompt: Explain why the cost of attention grows quadratically with sequence length, and what doubling the context does to it.
a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) every one of the n queries is scored against every one of the n keys, giving an n × n score matrix; (2) compute is about $n^2 d_k$ multiply-adds and the score matrix holds $n^2$ numbers; (3) doubling n multiplies this cost by 4, whereas the per-token projections and MLP grow only linearly.
a4-l009-scaled-dot-product.modelAnswer: Each of the $n$ tokens compares its query with all $n$ keys, so there are $n^2$ scores, each costing $d_k$ multiply-adds, and a naive implementation stores all $n^2$ of them. Doubling the context therefore quadruples attention's compute and score memory, while the linear layers only double. At long contexts attention dominates.

a4-l010-multi-head.prompt: A multi-head attention layer has model width $d=1024$ and 16 heads. Counting the query, key, value and output projections and ignoring biases, how many parameters does it have?
a4-l010-multi-head.explanation: $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ and $W_O$ are each $d\times d$ in total (each head uses a $d\times d/h$ slice), so the count is $4d^2=4{,}194{,}304$, independent of the number of heads.

a4-l010-multi-head.prompt: What does multi-head attention gain over one attention head of the same total width?
options: More parameters, which is the main source of its better accuracy over a single wide head.
A lower cost per layer, since each head's score matrix covers fewer tokens than one big head.
A longer usable context window, because each head is assigned its own separate segment of the input text.
Each head forms its own softmax pattern, so a layer can attend to several places for different reasons.
a4-l010-multi-head.explanation: Splitting into $h$ heads costs no extra parameters, but one softmax can only express one weighting over positions. With several heads, one can track the previous token while another tracks a verb's subject, and $W_O$ mixes their outputs back into the residual stream.

a4-l010-multi-head.prompt: Interpretability studies find 'previous-token heads' in trained transformers. What does such a head do?
options: At each position it puts most of its attention on the token just before.
It predicts the preceding token from the current one, reading text backwards.
It attends evenly to all earlier tokens, producing a running average of them.
It copies the first token of the sequence into every later position's output.
a4-l010-multi-head.explanation: A previous-token head writes 'the token before me was X' into each position. Other heads build on this; induction heads, for example, use it to complete repeated patterns. Heads that track syntax or coreference are other observed specializations.

a4-l010-multi-head.prompt: Explain how multi-head attention splits, runs and recombines its heads, and why its parameter count matches a single full-width head.
a4-l010-multi-head.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) each of h heads has its own Q, K, V projections of width d/h and computes its own attention; (2) head outputs (each n × d/h) are concatenated back to width d and multiplied by $W_O$ to mix them; (3) the h projections of width d/h together form d × d matrices, so Q, K, V and O total about $4d^2$, the same as one head of width d.
a4-l010-multi-head.modelAnswer: Each head projects the tokens to its own queries, keys and values of width $d/h$ and runs attention independently. The $h$ outputs are concatenated into a width-$d$ vector and $W_O$ mixes them. Since $h$ projections of width $d/h$ add up to one $d\times d$ matrix, the parameter count stays about $4d^2$; heads divide the width rather than adding to it.

a4-l011-positional-encodings.prompt: A self-attention layer with no positional information receives 'dog bites man' and then 'man bites dog'. How do its outputs compare?
options: The same three output vectors, reordered to follow the tokens.
Completely different vectors, since the weights depend on order.
An error, because keys cannot be computed without positions.
Identical except for the first token, which anchors the order.
a4-l011-positional-encodings.explanation: Without positions, each token's output depends only on its own vector and the unordered set of other tokens, so permuting the input permutes the output (permutation equivariance). The model cannot tell who bit whom, which is why position information must be added.

a4-l011-positional-encodings.prompt: Using sinusoidal positional encodings $PE_{(p,2i)}=\sin(p/10000^{2i/d})$ with model width $d=4$, what is the value at position $p=50$ in dimension $2i=2$? Give a decimal.
a4-l011-positional-encodings.explanation: $10000^{2/4}=100$, so the value is $\sin(50/100)=\sin 0.5\approx0.479$. Higher dimensions oscillate more slowly, so the encoding resembles a set of clock hands turning at geometrically spaced rates.

a4-l011-positional-encodings.prompt: Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) rotate query and key components by position-dependent angles. Why does the score $q\cdot k$ then depend only on the relative offset?
options: RoPE adds the offset $n-m$ to each score directly, after the dot product has been computed.
Only the keys are rotated, so the queries keep their absolute position and cancel it out.
Rotations stretch the vectors in proportion to position, so the distance is encoded in their length.
Rotating $q$ by $m\theta$ and $k$ by $n\theta$ leaves a dot product that depends on $(n-m)\theta$.
a4-l011-positional-encodings.explanation: Rotations preserve lengths, and $(R_mq)^{\top}(R_nk)=q^{\top}R_m^{\top}R_nk=q^{\top}R_{n-m}k$. Absolute positions cancel and only the offset remains, which suits language, where relative distance matters most.

a4-l011-positional-encodings.prompt: Explain why a transformer needs positional information at all, and contrast fixed sinusoidal encodings with learned absolute position embeddings.
a4-l011-positional-encodings.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) attention is permutation-equivariant, so without positions word order is invisible; (2) sinusoidal encodings are a fixed formula of sines and cosines at geometric frequencies, added to embeddings, with no parameters and defined for any position; (3) learned absolute embeddings are a trained vector per position, flexible but undefined beyond the maximum training length; (4) optionally, RoPE instead encodes relative offsets inside attention.
a4-l011-positional-encodings.modelAnswer: Attention treats its input as a set, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look the same without positions. Sinusoidal encodings add a fixed pattern of sines and cosines at many frequencies to each embedding: no parameters, and defined for any position. Learned absolute embeddings are a trained vector per position: flexible, but nothing exists for positions past the training length.

a4-l012-transformer-block.prompt: Apply LayerNorm (with $\gamma=1$, $\beta=0$, $\epsilon=0$) to $x=(1,2,3,6)$, using the population variance. What is the normalized value of the last entry? Give a decimal.
a4-l012-transformer-block.explanation: Mean $\mu=3$, variance $\sigma^2=(4+1+0+9)/4=3.5$, $\sigma=1.871$. The last entry becomes $(6-3)/1.871\approx1.60$. LayerNorm recentres and rescales each token's vector so the next layer sees inputs of a consistent scale.

a4-l012-transformer-block.prompt: Why do residual connections ($x\leftarrow x+f(x)$) keep 100-layer transformers trainable?
options: They double the number of parameters, which gives the optimizer more room to work.
They normalize every activation to unit variance, so neither activations nor gradients can explode.
The identity path gives gradients a direct route to early layers, so they do not vanish.
They let a layer skip its own training whenever the loss is already low enough.
a4-l012-transformer-block.explanation: Because each block adds to the stream rather than replacing it, the derivative of the output with respect to an early layer's output includes an identity term. Gradients reach the bottom of the stack without being multiplied through every layer. Normalization is LayerNorm's job, not the residual's.

a4-l012-transformer-block.prompt: In a standard transformer block whose MLP has hidden width $4d$, roughly what fraction of the block's parameters is in the MLP?
options: About one-third, since attention has four matrices.
About two-thirds: $8d^2$ out of roughly $12d^2$.
About one-half, since the two sublayers are equal.
Nearly all, since attention has no learned weights.
a4-l012-transformer-block.explanation: Attention has $W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O$, about $4d^2$. The MLP has a $d\times4d$ and a $4d\times d$ matrix, $8d^2$. So the MLP holds about $8/12$ of the block, which is why it is often described as the model's main store of learned associations.

a4-l012-transformer-block.prompt: Write the two residual updates of a pre-LayerNorm transformer block and explain the idea of the residual stream.
a4-l012-transformer-block.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $x\leftarrow x+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$ then $x\leftarrow x+\mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$; (2) the residual stream is a running vector per token that every sublayer reads from (after LayerNorm) and writes to by addition; (3) attention moves information between positions, the MLP processes each position separately; (4) the additive structure keeps an identity path for gradients and lets later layers use earlier layers' outputs directly.
a4-l012-transformer-block.modelAnswer: $x\leftarrow x+\mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$, then $x\leftarrow x+\mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$. Each token carries a vector, the residual stream, through the whole network. Every attention layer (which moves information between tokens) and every MLP (which transforms each token on its own) reads a normalized copy and adds its result back. Nothing is overwritten, so later layers can use anything earlier layers wrote, and gradients flow straight down the identity path.

a4-l013-causal-decoder.prompt: How does the causal mask let a single forward pass train a decoder on all $n$ next-token predictions at once?
options: It replaces the target token at each position with a [MASK] symbol that the model must then fill in.
Position $i$ cannot see tokens after $i$, so each output is an honest prediction of token $i+1$.
It forces the model to process tokens one at a time, which is how the $n$ predictions arise.
It zeroes the value vectors of future tokens but keeps their attention weights unchanged.
a4-l013-causal-decoder.explanation: Scores for $j>i$ are set to $-\infty$, so after softmax they get zero weight. Every position's output then depends only on its own prefix, exactly as at generation time, and all $n$ predictions can be scored against the shifted text in parallel.

a4-l013-causal-decoder.prompt: A GPT has $L=24$ layers, width $d=2048$ and vocabulary $V=50{,}000$. Using $N\approx12Ld^2+Vd$, estimate its parameter count. Give the answer in billions.
a4-l013-causal-decoder.explanation: $12\times24\times2048^2\approx1.208\times10^9$ in the blocks plus $50{,}000\times2048\approx0.102\times10^9$ in the embedding, about 1.31 billion. The $12d^2$ per layer is $4d^2$ of attention plus $8d^2$ of MLP.

a4-l013-causal-decoder.prompt: Which sequence describes a GPT-style forward pass?
options: Token ids → embedding lookup → $L$ blocks → final LayerNorm → unembedding → logits
Token ids → $L$ blocks → embedding lookup → final LayerNorm → softmax → logits
Token ids → unembedding → $L$ blocks → final LayerNorm → embedding lookup → logits
Token ids → embedding lookup → softmax → $L$ blocks → unembedding → logits
a4-l013-causal-decoder.explanation: Ids index the embedding table (plus position information), the residual stream passes through $L$ blocks, a final LayerNorm is applied, and the unembedding matrix $W_U$ maps each position's vector to $V$ logits. Softmax turns the last position's logits into the next-token distribution.

a4-l013-causal-decoder.prompt: Explain how the causal mask works mechanically, and why the same model trains in parallel but must generate one token at a time.
a4-l013-causal-decoder.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) scores $S_{ij}$ for $j>i$ are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, giving those keys zero weight; (2) each position then sees only its prefix, so in training all positions' next-token losses are computed in one pass (the targets are known); (3) at generation time the next token is unknown until sampled, so it must be produced and appended one step at a time.
a4-l013-causal-decoder.modelAnswer: Before the softmax, every score where a query would look at a later key is set to $-\infty$, so those keys get exactly zero weight. In training the whole text is known, so all $n$ positions can predict their next token in one parallel pass with no cheating. At generation the next token does not exist until it is sampled, so the model must generate it, append it and run again.

a4-l014-encoder-decoder.prompt: Which choice of architecture is best justified for each task: classifying molecules as toxic or not, translating IUPAC names into SMILES, and open-ended text generation?
options: Decoder-only; encoder; encoder–decoder
Encoder–decoder; decoder-only; encoder
Encoder; decoder-only; encoder–decoder
Encoder; encoder–decoder; decoder-only
a4-l014-encoder-decoder.explanation: A bidirectional encoder sees the whole input and suits classification. Translation maps one complete sequence to another, the classic encoder–decoder setting with cross-attention. Open-ended generation is what a causal decoder trained on next-token prediction does. Large decoders can do all three, but this is the natural fit.

a4-l014-encoder-decoder.prompt: In the cross-attention layer of an encoder–decoder model, where do queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries from the encoder output; keys and values from the decoder.
All three from the decoder, masked so it cannot see the encoder.
Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder output.
Queries and keys from the encoder; values from the decoder.
a4-l014-encoder-decoder.explanation: Each target position asks a question (query) and looks it up in the encoded source (keys), retrieving source information (values). This is how a translation model consults the input sentence while writing the output.

a4-l014-encoder-decoder.prompt: Contrast BERT-style encoders and GPT-style decoders by their attention masks and training objectives, and explain which one can generate open-ended text.
a4-l014-encoder-decoder.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) BERT: bidirectional (no causal mask) attention, trained with masked-language modelling, predicting hidden tokens from both sides; (2) GPT: causal mask, trained on next-token prediction from left context only; (3) only the causal decoder learns $P(w_t\mid w_{<t})$ and can generate text left to right; BERT's representations suit classification and extraction.
a4-l014-encoder-decoder.modelAnswer: BERT lets every token attend to every other and is trained to fill in randomly masked tokens using both sides of the context. This gives rich representations for classification but never learns to continue text. GPT uses a causal mask and learns to predict each token from its left context only, which is exactly the factorization needed to generate open-ended text one token at a time.

a4-l015-kv-cache.prompt: A model has $L=32$ layers, 8 key–value heads of dimension 128, and stores the cache in 16-bit floats. How much KV-cache memory does one 32,768-token sequence need? Give the answer in GiB ($2^{30}$ bytes).
a4-l015-kv-cache.explanation: $2\times32\times8\times128\times32768\times2=2^{32}$ bytes $=4$ GiB for a single sequence (the leading 2 counts keys and values). Serving many long conversations at once is limited by this memory, not by the weights.

a4-l015-kv-cache.prompt: During autoregressive generation, why can the keys and values of earlier tokens be cached and reused?
options: Under the causal mask earlier tokens never attend to later ones, so their keys and values never change.
Keys and values are identical in every layer, so one stored copy of them can serve all of the model's layers.
The cache stores the past attention weights, which are reused unchanged at every new step.
The cache stores the probabilities of earlier tokens, so they never need to be resampled.
a4-l015-kv-cache.explanation: A token's key and value in each layer depend only on its prefix, which does not change as new tokens are appended. Each new step therefore computes only the new token's query, key and value and attends over the cached ones: $O(n)$ work per step rather than recomputing the whole prefix.

a4-l015-kv-cache.prompt: What does FlashAttention change about attention?
options: It approximates the softmax with a cheaper function, trading a little accuracy for speed.
It drops low-weight keys and computes attention only over the few highest scores.
It shares one key–value head among all query heads to shrink the cache memory.
How the computation is tiled through fast on-chip memory; the output is unchanged.
a4-l015-kv-cache.explanation: FlashAttention processes queries and keys in tiles, keeping a running softmax normalizer, so the $n\times n$ score matrix is never written to slow GPU memory. The result is exact attention with far less memory traffic. Sharing KV heads is a different technique (multi-query or grouped-query attention).

a4-l015-kv-cache.prompt: Explain why generating each new token with a KV cache needs only $O(n)$ attention work, and how grouped-query attention reduces the cache's memory.
a4-l015-kv-cache.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) without a cache each step reruns the whole prefix; with it, only the new token's q, k, v are computed and the new query attends over n cached keys, so O(n) per step; (2) the cache size scales with layers × KV heads × head dim × context; (3) grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key–value head, cutting $n_{\text{kv}}$ and therefore cache memory and memory traffic, while attention itself is computed the same way.
a4-l015-kv-cache.modelAnswer: Past keys and values do not change, so each step only computes the new token's query, key and value and compares one query with $n$ cached keys: $O(n)$ rather than reprocessing the prefix. The cache grows with layers, KV heads, head size and context length. Grouped-query attention lets groups of query heads share one key–value head, so with 8 KV heads instead of 32 the cache is four times smaller.

a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.prompt: What does 'teacher forcing' mean when training a language model?
options: A larger teacher model's predicted outputs replace the raw text as the training targets for the student.
Only the final token of each document is used as a training target.
Each prediction conditions on the true previous tokens, not on the model's own outputs.
The learning rate follows a fixed schedule copied from an earlier training run.
a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.explanation: During training the prefix is always the real text, which is what lets all positions be trained in parallel. At generation time the model conditions on its own samples instead, so early mistakes can compound (exposure bias).

a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.prompt: Why does BERT's masked-language-model objective (mask about 15% of tokens) not directly support open-ended generation?
options: Masking only 15% of tokens gives too little signal to learn grammar or vocabulary.
It predicts hidden tokens from both sides, so it never learns to continue text left to right.
Its vocabulary has no end-of-sequence token, so during generation it could never decide when to stop.
It is trained on labelled data, which restricts it to classification tasks only.
a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.explanation: Generation needs $P(w_t\mid w_{<t})$. A masked model learns $P(\text{masked}\mid\text{both sides})$, a different conditional, so there is no natural way to sample a continuation. The causal objective trains exactly the factorization generation uses.

a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.prompt: A model assigns probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 to the three correct next tokens of a short text. What is its average next-token cross-entropy loss? Give the answer in nats.
a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.explanation: $-\frac13(\ln0.5+\ln0.25+\ln0.125)=\frac13(0.693+1.386+2.079)=1.386$ nats ($=2$ bits, a perplexity of 4). Training lowers this average over billions of tokens.

a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.prompt: Explain why pretraining a language model is called self-supervised, and why that matters for scale.
a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the targets come from the data itself: each next token (or masked token) is the label for its context; (2) so no human annotation is needed; (3) any raw text can be used, enabling training on trillions of tokens, far beyond what labelled datasets could supply.
a4-l016-pretraining-objectives.modelAnswer: In ordinary text, every token is the correct answer to 'what comes next?' given the tokens before it, so the data labels itself. No annotator is needed, which means any text on the web, in books or in code becomes training data. That is what makes trillion-token training runs possible, far beyond any hand-labelled dataset.

a4-l017-pretraining-data.prompt: A benchmark's test questions appear verbatim in the pretraining crawl. What is the main effect on the model's reported score?
options: No effect, since each document is seen only once in pretraining.
It overstates ability, since the model can recall memorized answers.
It understates ability, since memorized text disrupts reasoning.
Scores become noisier but remain unbiased estimates of ability on average.
a4-l017-pretraining-data.explanation: Contamination lets a model succeed by recall rather than by the skill the benchmark is meant to measure, so scores are inflated. Duplicated documents make memorization more likely, which is one reason pipelines deduplicate and test for benchmark overlap.

a4-l017-pretraining-data.prompt: A science corpus contains 3 billion English words (about 0.75 words per token). A training run of $10^{12}$ tokens gives this source a 2% mixture weight. About how many epochs over the corpus does the run make?
a4-l017-pretraining-data.explanation: The corpus is about $3\times10^9/0.75=4\times10^9$ tokens. The run draws $0.02\times10^{12}=2\times10^{10}$ tokens from it, so it sees the corpus about 5 times. Upweighting a small, high-quality source means repeating it, and too many repeats bring diminishing returns and memorization.

a4-l017-pretraining-data.prompt: Why do pretraining mixtures often weight code and scientific text far above their share of a raw web crawl?
options: Web text cannot be tokenized reliably, so code and papers have to replace it.
Code and papers contain no duplicates, so they can skip the filtering stage.
Copyright rules require most of any training corpus to come from those two kinds of source.
Mixture weights are tuned to build target abilities, such as reasoning and coding.
a4-l017-pretraining-data.explanation: Raw web proportions are an accident of what is online. Pipeline builders choose mixture weights by measuring downstream effects; code and science improve structured reasoning, so they are upsampled even though that means more epochs over them.

a4-l017-pretraining-data.prompt: Describe the main steps that turn a raw web crawl into a pretraining mix, and say what each step is for.
a4-l017-pretraining-data.rubric: Full credit requires most of: (1) text extraction from HTML (remove boilerplate, menus); (2) language identification; (3) quality filtering (heuristics or classifiers removing spam and low-quality text, plus safety filtering); (4) exact and near-duplicate removal, to avoid wasting compute and encouraging memorization; (5) decontamination against benchmarks; (6) mixture weights across web, code, books and science.
a4-l017-pretraining-data.modelAnswer: First extract the main text from HTML, dropping menus and boilerplate. Identify the language so each can be handled and balanced. Filter for quality with rules and classifiers to remove spam and junk. Deduplicate exact and near-identical pages so nothing is seen far more often than it deserves, and remove benchmark text. Finally set mixture weights across web, code, books and science to target the abilities you want.

a4-l018-training-at-scale.prompt: Estimate the GPU-days needed to train a 7-billion-parameter model on $2\times10^{12}$ tokens using $C\approx6ND$, if each GPU sustains $4\times10^{14}$ FLOP/s.
a4-l018-training-at-scale.explanation: $C=6\times7\times10^9\times2\times10^{12}=8.4\times10^{22}$ FLOPs. One GPU-day is $4\times10^{14}\times86{,}400\approx3.46\times10^{19}$ FLOPs, so about 2,400 GPU-days, e.g. 256 GPUs for roughly 9.5 days. The 6 counts 2 FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass.

a4-l018-training-at-scale.prompt: Which matching of technique to what it splits or shrinks is correct?
options: Data parallel: the batch · Tensor parallel: each weight matrix · Pipeline parallel: the layers · bf16: bytes per value
Data parallel: the layers · Tensor parallel: the batch · Pipeline parallel: each weight matrix · bf16: bytes per value
Data parallel: the batch · Tensor parallel: the layers · Pipeline parallel: each weight matrix · bf16: the batch size
Data parallel: each weight matrix · Tensor parallel: the batch · Pipeline parallel: the layers · bf16: the layer count
a4-l018-training-at-scale.explanation: Data parallelism gives each GPU a full model copy and a slice of the batch, then averages gradients. Tensor parallelism splits individual matrix multiplications across GPUs; pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive layers to different GPUs. bf16 stores values in 2 bytes instead of 4, halving memory and bandwidth while keeping fp32's exponent range.

a4-l018-training-at-scale.prompt: Why does AdamW apply weight decay directly to the parameters rather than adding $\lambda\theta$ to the gradient?
options: Adding it to the gradient would make the loss non-differentiable wherever a weight is exactly zero.
Decoupling lets the decay switch off during warmup, which is needed for the run to stay stable.
Added to the gradient, the decay would be rescaled by Adam's per-parameter step size and act unevenly.
On the gradient, weight decay turns into an L1 penalty and drives most of the weights to exactly zero.
a4-l018-training-at-scale.explanation: Adam divides each gradient component by $\sqrt{\hat v_t}$. Decay added to the gradient gets divided too, so weights with large gradient history are barely decayed. AdamW subtracts $\eta\lambda\theta$ separately, giving the uniform shrinkage that weight decay is meant to provide.

a4-l018-training-at-scale.prompt: Explain in your own words what the parts of the AdamW update do ($m_t$, $v_t$, the ratio $\hat m_t/\sqrt{\hat v_t}$, the decay term), and why transformers use linear warmup followed by cosine decay of the learning rate.
a4-l018-training-at-scale.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $m_t$ is a running mean of gradients (momentum, smoothing noise); (2) $v_t$ is a running mean of squared gradients; dividing by $\sqrt{\hat v_t}$ gives each parameter a step of roughly fixed size regardless of gradient scale; (3) hats denote bias correction; $\lambda\theta$ is decoupled weight decay; (4) warmup: early moment estimates are unreliable and the network is in a sensitive state, so large steps at the start can diverge; (5) cosine decay lowers the rate smoothly so the loss can settle into a minimum at the end.
a4-l018-training-at-scale.modelAnswer: $m_t$ averages recent gradients, giving momentum that smooths noise. $v_t$ averages squared gradients, and dividing by $\sqrt{\hat v_t}$ normalizes each parameter's step so rarely-updated and noisy parameters move at similar rates; the hats correct the bias from starting at zero. The $\lambda\theta$ term shrinks weights directly. Warmup ramps the rate up from near zero because early second-moment estimates are poor and big early steps can blow training up. Cosine decay then lowers the rate smoothly so training settles.

a4-l019-scaling-laws.prompt: On a log–log plot, loss follows a straight line $L=(N_c/N)^{\alpha}$, falling from 3.0 at $N=10^8$ parameters to 2.4 at $N=10^{10}$. What is the exponent $\alpha$? Give a decimal.
a4-l019-scaling-laws.explanation: $\alpha=\ln(3.0/2.4)/\ln(10^{10}/10^8)=0.223/4.605\approx0.048$, the negative of the line's slope. A hundredfold increase in parameters buys only a 20% lower loss, which is why scaling is so expensive.

a4-l019-scaling-laws.prompt: In the Chinchilla fit $L(N,D)=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta}$, what does the constant $E$ represent?
options: The error caused by the optimizer, which a better training recipe removes.
The loss of a model with no parameters, which guesses uniformly at random.
The loss left with infinite parameters and data, set by the text's own entropy.
A fitting constant with no physical meaning beyond making the curve match the data points.
a4-l019-scaling-laws.explanation: Natural text is inherently unpredictable: even a perfect model cannot know which of several valid continuations comes next. $E$ estimates that irreducible entropy. The other two terms are the excess loss from finite model size and finite data, each falling as a power law.

a4-l019-scaling-laws.prompt: A power law fitted on models up to 1B parameters is used to predict the loss of a 30B model. Which is the strongest reason the prediction might fail?
options: Power laws can never be extrapolated, since they are only valid on the fitted range.
Training the larger model may exhaust fresh data, forcing repeats the fit never saw.
Bigger models always beat the fit, because new abilities emerge abruptly at scale.
Log–log axes exaggerate small differences, so the fitted slope cannot be trusted.
a4-l019-scaling-laws.explanation: Scaling laws hold empirically when the conditions of the fit stay the same. A larger run may run out of unique data, change the data mix, or change architecture or optimizer, and any of these can bend the curve. Extrapolating over modest ranges under fixed conditions has often worked well.

a4-l019-scaling-laws.prompt: Explain what each term of the Chinchilla scaling law $L(N,D)=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta}$ means, and how it differs from a Kaplan-style law $L(N)=(N_c/N)^{\alpha_N}$.
a4-l019-scaling-laws.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) E is the irreducible loss (entropy of the data) that remains as N, D → ∞; (2) $A/N^{\alpha}$ is excess loss from finite model capacity; (3) $B/D^{\beta}$ is excess loss from finite data; (4) Kaplan's form describes loss vs one resource at a time, with no floor, so it falls toward zero; Chinchilla's joint form has a floor and lets you trade N against D for a fixed budget.
a4-l019-scaling-laws.modelAnswer: $E$ is the floor: the entropy of language that no model can remove. $A/N^{\alpha}$ is the extra loss because the model is too small to capture everything, and $B/D^{\beta}$ is the extra loss because it has not seen enough data; both shrink as power laws. Kaplan's law tracks loss against one resource with no floor, so taken literally it goes to zero. The joint Chinchilla form includes the floor and shows how to split a budget between $N$ and $D$.

a4-l020-compute-optimal.prompt: With a compute budget of $C=10^{24}$ FLOPs, $C\approx6ND$ and the Chinchilla rule $D\approx20N$, how many training tokens should a compute-optimal run use? Give the answer in trillions of tokens.
a4-l020-compute-optimal.explanation: Substituting $D=20N$ gives $C=120N^2$, so $N=\sqrt{10^{24}/120}\approx9.1\times10^{10}$ parameters and $D=20N\approx1.83\times10^{12}$ tokens. A budget a hundred times larger would multiply each by ten.

a4-l020-compute-optimal.prompt: Many recent open models are trained on 100 or more tokens per parameter, far past the Chinchilla ratio. Why?
options: Serving cost scales with model size, so a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to use.
Chinchilla's result was overturned, so 20 tokens per parameter is too few for any model.
Overtraining reduces the total training compute needed to reach any given level of loss.
Small models cannot learn anything from short runs, so they need extra data just to train at all.
a4-l020-compute-optimal.explanation: Chinchilla minimizes loss per unit of training compute. A widely used model spends far more compute on inference than on training, and inference cost scales with $N$. Training a smaller model well past 20 tokens per parameter costs extra training compute but gives a cheaper model of similar quality.

a4-l020-compute-optimal.prompt: For $L=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta}$ with $\alpha=\beta$, minimizing $L$ at fixed $C=6ND$ gives how $N_{\text{opt}}$ and $D_{\text{opt}}$ scale with $C$?
options: $N\propto C$ with $D$ fixed: extra compute should go into parameters.
$D\propto C$ with $N$ fixed: extra compute should go into more data.
$N\propto C^{1/3}$ and $D\propto C^{2/3}$: data should grow faster than size.
Both as $C^{1/2}$: ten times the compute means $\sqrt{10}$ times each.
a4-l020-compute-optimal.explanation: With equal exponents the two terms are symmetric, and the Lagrange condition makes $A/N^{\alpha}$ and $B/D^{\beta}$ proportional at the optimum. Then $N$ and $D$ grow in a fixed ratio, so each grows as $C^{1/2}$. Chinchilla's fitted exponents gave $a\approx b\approx0.5$.

a4-l020-compute-optimal.prompt: Explain in words the Lagrange-multiplier argument for the compute-optimal split between parameters $N$ and tokens $D$ under a fixed budget $C=6ND$.
a4-l020-compute-optimal.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) minimize L(N, D) subject to 6ND = C; (2) at the optimum the gradient of L is parallel to the gradient of the constraint, i.e. the marginal loss reduction per unit of compute is equal whether spent on more parameters or more tokens; (3) if one were larger you could move compute toward it and lower the loss; (4) with power-law terms this gives $N_{\text{opt}}\propto C^{a}$, $D_{\text{opt}}\propto C^{b}$ (both about 0.5 for Chinchilla).
a4-l020-compute-optimal.modelAnswer: We minimize $L(N,D)$ along the curve $6ND=C$. At the optimum, the last FLOP spent on parameters must reduce the loss exactly as much as the last FLOP spent on data; otherwise moving compute from one to the other would lower the loss. That equal-marginal-benefit condition is what the Lagrange multiplier enforces, and with power-law terms it makes $N$ and $D$ each grow as a power of $C$, about $C^{0.5}$.

a4-l021-emergence.prompt: A task requires a 20-token answer to be exactly right, and tokens are independent. If scaling raises per-token accuracy from 0.90 to 0.95, what is the new exact-match accuracy? Give a decimal.
a4-l021-emergence.explanation: $0.95^{20}\approx0.36$, up from $0.90^{20}\approx0.12$. A modest, smooth gain per token triples the task score, and on a plot against model size such jumps look sudden.

a4-l021-emergence.prompt: What is the main counter-argument to claims that some abilities 'emerge' abruptly at a critical model size?
options: Larger models are tested on easier subsets of benchmarks, which inflates their scores.
The jumps are real and caused by the training loss itself dropping at a critical size.
Exact-match scoring gives no partial credit, so smooth per-token gains can look like a jump.
Small models have much noisier losses, which hides an ability that they already possess in full.
a4-l021-emergence.explanation: When the metric is all-or-nothing over many tokens, a steadily improving per-token probability maps to a sharply rising curve. Re-scoring with continuous metrics (log-likelihood of the answer, partial credit) often makes the same abilities improve smoothly.

a4-l021-emergence.prompt: Which way of scoring would most likely make an apparently 'emergent' ability look like smooth improvement?
options: The log-probability the model gives the correct answer.
Exact-match accuracy with a stricter answer format.
Pass or fail on only the single hardest test problem.
Accuracy measured on a smaller but much cleaner test set.
a4-l021-emergence.explanation: Continuous metrics track the underlying per-token improvement directly. Thresholded metrics (exact match, pass/fail) hide progress until the probability of getting everything right becomes appreciable, which produces the hockey-stick shape.

a4-l021-emergence.prompt: Explain why a smooth decrease in pretraining loss does not tell you directly when a model will become good at a particular task.
a4-l021-emergence.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) loss is an average over all tokens, while a task depends on a small subset of skills and tokens; (2) task metrics are often thresholded (exact match over k tokens), so accuracy behaves like $p^k$ and stays near zero until p is high, then rises steeply; (3) so the relation between loss and task accuracy is nonlinear and task-specific, and apparent emergence may partly reflect the metric.
a4-l021-emergence.modelAnswer: Pretraining loss averages surprise over every token of every kind of text, but a task depends on a narrow skill. Task scores are often all-or-nothing: a 20-token answer is right with probability about $p^{20}$, which stays near zero until per-token accuracy is high and then climbs fast. So loss can fall smoothly while task accuracy sits flat and then shoots up, and the shape depends on the metric as much as the model.

a4-l022-decoding.prompt: A next-token distribution is A 0.50, B 0.20, C 0.15, D 0.10, E 0.05. With nucleus (top-$p$) sampling at $p=0.8$, the smallest set of top tokens reaching 0.8 is kept and renormalized. What probability does B then get? Give a decimal.
a4-l022-decoding.explanation: Cumulative mass is 0.50, 0.70, 0.85, so the nucleus is {A, B, C} (0.70 alone falls short). Renormalizing gives B $0.20/0.85\approx0.235$. Top-$k$ with $k=2$ would keep only {A, B}, whatever their mass.

a4-l022-decoding.prompt: Why does greedy decoding often fall into repeating the same phrase?
options: Greedy decoding is sampling at infinite temperature, which spreads probability onto filler words.
Once a phrase repeats, repeating it again tends to become the most likely continuation.
Greedy decoding discards the KV cache between steps, so the model forgets what it already wrote.
Greedy decoding draws tokens at random from the whole vocabulary, so stock phrases keep recurring.
a4-l022-decoding.explanation: Greedy and beam search pick high-probability tokens, and models assign high probability to continuing patterns already in the context, so loops reinforce themselves. Pure sampling avoids loops but wanders into low-probability tokens; temperature, top-$k$ and top-$p$ trade between the two.

a4-l022-decoding.prompt: Why can the same prompt at temperature 0 sometimes give different outputs from a hosted model?
options: Temperature 0 still samples, just from a very narrow distribution around the top token.
Providers add random noise to the logits for privacy, even when temperature is set to 0.
The tokenizer splits the same prompt differently on each request to balance the load.
Batching and kernel choices change floating-point rounding, which can flip a near-tie.
a4-l022-decoding.explanation: Floating-point addition is not associative, so summing in a different order (different batch sizes or GPU kernels) gives slightly different logits. When two tokens are nearly tied, the argmax can flip, and generation diverges from there.

a4-l022-decoding.prompt: Explain how the sampling temperature trades diversity against fidelity, using the Boltzmann picture.
a4-l022-decoding.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $p_i\propto e^{z_i/T}$ is a Boltzmann distribution with logits as negative energies; (2) low T concentrates on the top tokens (ground state): faithful, likely text but repetitive and low diversity, T → 0 is greedy; (3) high T flattens the distribution, populating 'high-energy' unlikely tokens: more diverse but more errors and incoherence; (4) truncation methods (top-k, top-p) cut off the unlikely tail.
a4-l022-decoding.modelAnswer: Sampling uses $p_i\propto e^{z_i/T}$, a Boltzmann distribution over tokens with logits as negative energies. At low temperature only the lowest-energy states (the most likely tokens) are populated: output is safe and accurate but bland and repetitive, and $T\to0$ is greedy decoding. Raising $T$ populates unlikely tokens too, giving variety at the cost of more mistakes and drift. Top-$k$ and top-$p$ remove the far tail so moderate temperatures stay coherent.

a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.prompt: A mixture-of-experts model has 2 billion shared parameters (attention, embeddings) plus 64 expert MLPs of 100 million parameters each, and routes each token to its top 2 experts. How many parameters are active per token? Give the answer in billions.
a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.explanation: Active $=2\text{B}+2\times0.1\text{B}=2.2$ billion, while the total is $2\text{B}+64\times0.1\text{B}=8.4$ billion. Compute per token scales with the active count; memory must hold the total.

a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.prompt: Why do mixture-of-experts models add an auxiliary load-balancing loss?
options: Otherwise the gate values would not sum to one across the chosen experts for each token.
Otherwise tokens could be sent to more than $k$ experts at once, which multiplies the compute cost.
Otherwise early-favoured experts get more tokens and training, so the router keeps choosing them.
Otherwise all of the experts learn the same function, which wastes their extra capacity.
a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.explanation: Routing is self-reinforcing: an expert that gets more tokens improves faster and wins even more of them, so a few experts end up doing everything while the rest sit idle. The auxiliary loss penalizes uneven usage across experts and keeps capacity in use.

a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.prompt: Compared with a dense model with the same total number of parameters, an MoE model of that size:
options: Uses less memory, because only the active experts need to be stored.
Saves both FLOPs and memory per token, with no trade-off in serving.
Uses more FLOPs, because every expert runs and the router then picks one output.
Uses far fewer FLOPs per token but must still hold all experts in memory.
a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.explanation: Only the top-$k$ experts run for each token, so compute tracks active parameters. But any token might be routed to any expert, so all of them must be resident in memory. MoE trades memory (and communication) for compute.

a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.prompt: Explain how a mixture-of-experts layer decides which experts process a token and how their outputs are combined.
a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a router (a learned linear map $W_r$) computes a score per expert for the token, and a softmax turns scores into gates; (2) only the top-k experts by gate are run (sparse activation); (3) the output is the gate-weighted sum of those experts' MLP outputs, $y=\sum_{i\in\text{top-}k}g_i E_i(x)$; (4) different tokens can go to different experts, so capacity grows without growing per-token compute.
a4-l023-mixture-of-experts.modelAnswer: A small learned router multiplies the token's vector by $W_r$ to get one score per expert and applies a softmax to get gate weights. Only the $k$ experts with the largest gates run; each is an ordinary MLP. Their outputs are added, weighted by the gates. Different tokens choose different experts, so the model holds many parameters while each token uses only a few.

a4-l024-fine-tuning.prompt: You have only 200 labelled examples for a new classification task and a large pretrained model. Which approach is usually safest?
options: Fine-tune all weights at a high learning rate so the task is learned fast.
Freeze the backbone and train a small linear head on its features.
Train a fresh model from scratch, since pretrained features rarely transfer.
Fine-tune only the embedding table, where the domain knowledge is stored.
a4-l024-fine-tuning.explanation: A frozen backbone already provides useful features, and a linear head has few parameters, so 200 examples are enough without overfitting. Full fine-tuning adapts more but needs more data and care. Transfer learning works because pretrained features are general.

a4-l024-fine-tuning.prompt: Which recipe best limits catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning on a narrow task?
options: A small learning rate, few epochs, and some general data mixed into the task data.
A large learning rate, so the task is learned before forgetting has time to start.
Many epochs on the task data alone, so the new skill is consolidated before stopping.
Turning off weight decay, so the pretrained weights are free to move where needed.
a4-l024-fine-tuning.explanation: Forgetting happens when large or prolonged updates on narrow data overwrite weights that encoded general abilities. Small, short updates stay near the pretrained solution, and replaying general data keeps the old abilities in the loss.

a4-l024-fine-tuning.prompt: A lab has measured yields for 30,000 of its own reactions and wants to predict yields for new runs. Should it fine-tune a model or rely on prompting a general LLM? Justify the choice by data size and cost.
a4-l024-fine-tuning.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a reasoned choice, typically fine-tuning (or training a smaller specialized model/head) given tens of thousands of labelled examples; (2) prompting can fit only a handful of examples in context and general LLMs are poor at precise numeric regression on proprietary chemistry; (3) cost: fine-tuning has an up-front cost but cheaper, more accurate predictions per query; prompting suits tasks with little data or that change often; (4) mentions evaluation on held-out (e.g. scaffold-split) reactions.
a4-l024-fine-tuning.modelAnswer: Fine-tune. Thirty thousand labelled reactions is far more than fits in a prompt, and a general model has never seen this lab's conditions; precise yield regression is not something prompting does well. A fine-tuned model, or a frozen pretrained chemistry encoder with a trained regression head, learns the lab's own patterns once, then predicts cheaply. Prompting makes sense when there are only a few examples or the task keeps changing. Either way, test on reactions held out by scaffold or substrate class.

a4-l025-instruction-tuning.prompt: In supervised fine-tuning on (instruction, response) pairs, the loss is computed only on response tokens. Why?
options: Prompt tokens have no next-token labels, so a loss on them simply cannot be computed at all.
Masking the prompt doubles the effective learning rate on the response tokens.
Training on prompt tokens would leak each answer into the model's input sequence.
The goal is to learn to produce responses, not to imitate the prompts users will write.
a4-l025-instruction-tuning.explanation: Prompt tokens do have next-token targets, but training on them spends capacity on modelling user text. Masking focuses the gradient on what the assistant should say given the prompt: $\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{t\in\text{response}}\log p(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})$.

a4-l025-instruction-tuning.prompt: A chat-tuned model is given raw text without its chat template's special tokens marking the user and assistant turns. What typically happens?
options: Nothing changes, since the tokenizer strips special tokens anyway.
Quality drops: it may continue the user's text rather than answer it.
It refuses, because unmarked input is treated as a jailbreak attempt.
It works better, since template tokens only waste context space.
a4-l025-instruction-tuning.explanation: Instruction tuning teaches the model to respond after the assistant-turn marker. The template's special tokens tell it who is speaking and where its reply begins; without them the input looks like a document to continue, the pretraining behaviour.

a4-l025-instruction-tuning.prompt: Explain why instruction tuning changes a model's format and helpfulness much more than it changes what the model knows.
a4-l025-instruction-tuning.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) SFT datasets are small (thousands to millions of examples) compared with trillions of pretraining tokens, so they cannot add much knowledge; (2) what they teach is a style and behaviour: follow instructions, answer in the assistant role, use formats; (3) knowledge comes from pretraining; SFT selects and surfaces it (the 'superficial alignment' view); (4) fine-tuning on facts the model does not already know can even encourage hallucination.
a4-l025-instruction-tuning.modelAnswer: Pretraining saw trillions of tokens; instruction tuning adds perhaps thousands to millions of examples. That is far too little to teach much new knowledge, but plenty to teach a behaviour: read the request, answer as an assistant, follow the requested format, stop when done. The knowledge was already there; instruction tuning teaches the model how to surface it on request.

a4-l026-lora.prompt: LoRA with rank $r=8$ is applied to a $4096\times4096$ weight matrix. What percentage of that matrix's parameters is trainable? Give the answer in percent.
a4-l026-lora.explanation: $r(d+k)/(dk)=8\times8192/4096^2\approx0.0039$, about 0.39%. $B$ is $4096\times8$ and $A$ is $8\times4096$: 65,536 trainable numbers instead of 16.8 million.

a4-l026-lora.prompt: Why is LoRA's matrix $B$ initialized to zero (with $A$ random)?
options: It keeps the update rank zero for good, which prevents overfitting.
It keeps every LoRA gradient at zero until $A$ has converged.
Then $BA=0$, so training starts exactly from the pretrained model.
It applies the $\alpha/r$ scaling so that larger ranks do not diverge.
a4-l026-lora.explanation: With $B=0$ the adapted weight $W_0+(\alpha/r)BA$ equals $W_0$ at step 0, so fine-tuning begins at the pretrained solution with no random disturbance. The gradient with respect to $B$ is nonzero (it involves $A$), so $B$ starts learning immediately.

a4-l026-lora.prompt: After fine-tuning, why can a LoRA adapter add no extra latency at inference?
options: $W_0+(\alpha/r)BA$ can be computed once and stored as one ordinary matrix.
The adapter runs on a separate GPU, in parallel with the base model's layers.
LoRA replaces $W_0$ with the product $BA$, which is a smaller matrix to apply.
The adapter is used only while training and is discarded before deployment.
a4-l026-lora.explanation: Merging folds the low-rank update into the weights, giving a model with the original shape and speed. Alternatively, keeping adapters separate lets one base model serve many tasks by swapping small adapters, at a small cost per request.

a4-l026-lora.prompt: Connect LoRA to the low-rank (truncated SVD) approximation of a matrix, and explain why a low-rank update is often enough for fine-tuning.
a4-l026-lora.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) any $d\times k$ matrix can be approximated by its top r singular components, $U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\top}$, a rank-r product of a $d\times r$ and an $r\times k$ factor; (2) LoRA learns the update $\Delta W=BA$ directly in that rank-r form; (3) empirically the weight changes needed to adapt a pretrained model have low intrinsic rank, because the model already has the needed features and only a few directions need adjusting; (4) so few parameters suffice and adapters are small to store and swap.
a4-l026-lora.modelAnswer: Truncated SVD says the best rank-$r$ approximation of a matrix keeps its $r$ largest singular directions, a product of a tall $d\times r$ and a wide $r\times k$ factor. LoRA restricts the fine-tuning update to exactly that form, $\Delta W=BA$. It works because adapting a capable pretrained model mostly re-weights a few directions it already has; the needed change has low intrinsic rank, so a few thousand parameters per matrix capture most of it.

a4-l027-quantization.prompt: The weight block $w=(0.8,\,-0.3,\,0.05,\,-1.2)$ is quantized to signed int4 with scale $s=\max|w|/(2^{b-1}-1)$ and $q=\mathrm{round}(w/s)$. What value does the weight 0.8 have after dequantizing ($q\,s$)? Give a decimal.
a4-l027-quantization.explanation: $s=1.2/7\approx0.1714$. Then $0.8/s\approx4.67$ rounds to 5, which dequantizes to $5s\approx0.857$, an error of about 0.057 (up to $s/2$). One large weight sets the scale for the whole block, which is why small per-block scales are used.

a4-l027-quantization.prompt: Roughly how much memory do the weights of a 7-billion-parameter model need in fp16, int8 and int4?
options: 7 GB, 3.5 GB and 1.75 GB
14 GB, 7 GB and 3.5 GB
28 GB, 14 GB and 7 GB
14 GB in all three formats
a4-l027-quantization.explanation: Bytes $=N\times b/8$: 2 bytes, 1 byte and half a byte per parameter. 28 GB would be fp32. The KV cache and activations come on top of the weights.

a4-l027-quantization.prompt: In QLoRA, which parts of the model are trained?
options: The 4-bit base weights, with LoRA used afterwards to fix the rounding error.
