Autoregressive models discretize images into tokens and generate them in sequence like text. Speech models similarly turn audio into discrete tokens with a neural codec so a transformer can model them.

a4-l053-vision-language-models.prompt: Name three uses of multimodal models in chemistry and the typical failure mode of each.
a4-l053-vision-language-models.rubric: Full credit requires three uses with a plausible failure each, e.g.: (1) reading spectra (NMR, IR, MS images): misreading peak positions or multiplicities, inventing peaks; (2) reading reaction schemes: missing reagents above arrows or conditions, mis-assigning which arrow belongs to which step; (3) structure images to SMILES (optical chemical structure recognition): dropping stereochemistry (wedges and dashes), misreading small subscripts, charges or abbreviations such as Ph or Boc; (4) extracting tables and plots: misreading axes or values. Noting the need to verify outputs.
a4-l053-vision-language-models.modelAnswer: Reading spectra from figures: the model may misread chemical shifts or coupling patterns, or describe peaks that are not there. Extracting reaction schemes from papers: reagents and conditions written above arrows get dropped or attached to the wrong step. Converting drawn structures to SMILES: wedge and dash stereochemistry, small charges and abbreviations such as OTBS are often lost or misread. In all three, check the output against the original.

a4-l054-molecules-proteins.prompt: Why does every SELFIES string decode to a valid molecule, while random edits to a SMILES string often do not?
options: SELFIES strings are shorter, so there are fewer places for errors.
SELFIES models are trained for longer, so they make fewer mistakes.
SELFIES store only atoms and let the decoder choose bonds freely.
SELFIES' grammar is built so any token sequence obeys valence rules.
a4-l054-molecules-proteins.explanation: SMILES has syntax that must pair up: ring-closure digits must match, parentheses must balance, and valences must work out, so a random character change often breaks it. SELFIES tokens are interpreted by a state machine that tracks remaining valence and only forms allowed bonds, so every sequence is a valid molecule, which is convenient for generative models.

a4-l054-molecules-proteins.prompt: A toxicity model scores 0.95 AUC on a random split of a dataset but 0.70 on a scaffold split of the same data. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The scaffold split must be buggy, since a good model scores the same on any split of the data.
Random splits put close analogues in both train and test, so 0.95 overstates generalization.
Scaffold splits are easier, so the 0.70 means the model is underfitting the training data.
The random split leaks the label through the SMILES string, which a scaffold split hides.
a4-l054-molecules-proteins.explanation: Molecules from the same series share scaffolds and similar labels. In a random split, test compounds have near-twins in training, so performance reflects interpolation. A scaffold split holds out whole chemotypes, which is closer to predicting new chemistry. Claims should also be compared with simple baselines such as fingerprints with a random forest.

a4-l054-molecules-proteins.prompt: Explain how transformers treat molecules (SMILES) and proteins (amino-acid sequences) as languages, and what masked-language-model pretraining learns from them without labels.
a4-l054-molecules-proteins.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) molecules and proteins are written as strings over an alphabet (SMILES or SELFIES characters; 20 amino acids), so they can be tokenized and modelled with the same transformer machinery as text; (2) masked-LM pretraining hides tokens and predicts them from context, on large unlabelled corpora; (3) to do this the model must learn chemical grammar and regularities: valence, common functional groups and ring systems for molecules; for proteins, which residues co-vary, which encodes structural contacts, and evolutionary constraints; (4) the learned embeddings transfer to property or structure prediction with few labels.
a4-l054-molecules-proteins.modelAnswer: A SMILES string or a protein sequence is a string over a small alphabet, so it can be tokenized and fed to a transformer like text. In masked-language-model pretraining, tokens are hidden and the model predicts them from the rest, with no labels needed. To fill in a masked atom it must learn valence, functional groups and ring patterns; to fill in a masked residue it must learn which positions co-vary across evolution, which reflects which residues touch in the folded structure. Those embeddings then transfer to property or structure prediction with little labelled data.

a4-l055-probing.prompt: Why should a probing study also train the probe on a control task, such as randomly assigned labels?
options: A control task checks that the language model itself was trained correctly in the first place.
A control task identifies which layer of the model actually computes the property.
A control task removes the need for a held-out test set when evaluating the probe.
A probe can learn the task itself; a control shows how much is due to the representation.
a4-l055-probing.explanation: A flexible probe can memorize arbitrary word-to-label mappings, so high accuracy alone does not prove the representation encodes the property. 'Selectivity', the accuracy on the real task minus that on the control, shows how much the representation helps. Simple linear probes have low capacity for this reason.

a4-l055-probing.prompt: A linear probe recovers 'contains an aromatic ring' from layer 12 of a chemistry model with 98% accuracy. What does this establish?
options: The model relies on aromaticity whenever it makes its downstream predictions.
Layer 12 is the layer where aromaticity is first computed.
The information is linearly decodable there, not that the model uses it.
The model understands aromaticity in the same way chemists do.
a4-l055-probing.explanation: Probing is correlational: the property can be read out, but the model might never use that direction downstream. Causal tests, such as ablating or patching the direction and watching outputs change, are needed to show the model uses it.

a4-l055-probing.prompt: Explain the difference between information being decodable from a model's activations and the model actually using it, and describe a causal test that distinguishes the two.
a4-l055-probing.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) decodable: a probe can predict the property from hidden states, which shows the information is present (possibly incidentally); (2) used: the model's outputs depend on that information; (3) a causal test, e.g. ablation (remove or zero the probe direction and see whether behaviour that needs the property degrades) or activation patching or steering (swap in activations from an input with a different property value and see whether the output changes accordingly); (4) if intervening changes behaviour as predicted, the representation is used.
a4-l055-probing.modelAnswer: Decodable means a probe can read the property from the activations: the information is there, perhaps only as a by-product. Used means the model's later computation depends on it. To tell them apart, intervene: project out the probe's direction (ablation) and see whether outputs that need the property get worse, or patch in activations from an input where the property differs and see whether the output flips. Only an intervention that changes behaviour shows the model relies on that information.

a4-l056-logit-lens.prompt: Applying the unembedding to the residual stream after each layer (the 'logit lens') typically shows what?
options: Vague early guesses that sharpen toward the final prediction in later layers.
The final prediction already exact at layer 1, unchanged through the stack.
Random tokens at every layer until the last, then a jump to the answer.
The input token itself at each layer, with no hint of the next token.
a4-l056-logit-lens.explanation: Because every layer adds to one residual stream that ends at the unembedding, intermediate states can be read in the same vocabulary basis. Middle layers often already rank the eventual answer highly, and later layers refine it. Very early layers are harder to read this way, which variants such as the tuned lens address.

a4-l056-logit-lens.prompt: Direct logit attribution splits a final logit difference (correct minus incorrect token) into contributions: embedding 0.2, attention head A 1.5, head B $-0.4$, MLP layer 2.1. What fraction of the total logit difference comes from head A? Give a decimal.
a4-l056-logit-lens.explanation: Total $=0.2+1.5-0.4+2.1=3.4$, so head A contributes $1.5/3.4\approx0.44$. Head B works against the answer. Contributions simply add because the residual stream is a sum and the unembedding is linear.

a4-l056-logit-lens.prompt: Why can the final logits be split into additive contributions from each attention head and MLP layer?
options: Each head writes into its own reserved slice of the residual stream.
The residual stream is a sum of their outputs, and the unembedding is linear.
The softmax is linear, so output probabilities can be added directly.
Heads never interact, so their ablation effects sum to the logits.
a4-l056-logit-lens.explanation: $x_L=x_0+\sum(\text{attn}_\ell+\text{mlp}_\ell)$, and $W_U$ distributes over the sum. The final LayerNorm is nonlinear, so attributions freeze its scale factor at the value from the actual run. This gives each component's direct effect; indirect effects through later layers need other methods.

a4-l056-logit-lens.prompt: Explain how the residual stream's structure makes the logit lens and direct logit attribution possible.
a4-l056-logit-lens.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) every layer reads from and adds to the residual stream, so the final state is the embedding plus a sum of all component outputs; (2) the unembedding $W_U$ is a linear map applied (after LayerNorm) to that final state, so any intermediate state, which is a partial sum, can be pushed through it to see the prediction so far (logit lens); (3) by linearity, the logits split into a term for each component's output (with the LayerNorm scale frozen), which is direct logit attribution; (4) caveat: this captures direct effects only.
a4-l056-logit-lens.modelAnswer: Each layer adds its output into the same running vector, so the final residual state is the embedding plus the sum of every head's and MLP's contribution, and the logits are a linear map ($W_U$ after LayerNorm) of that sum. Stopping partway gives a partial sum that can go through the same map, which is the logit lens. Because the map is linear (freezing the LayerNorm scale), it also distributes over the sum, so each component's output yields its own slice of the logits: direct logit attribution. It misses effects that pass through later layers.

a4-l057-superposition.prompt: What does the linear representation hypothesis claim?
options: Each neuron represents exactly one human-interpretable feature of the input.
Features are stored only in specific attention heads, never in the MLP layers.
Features are directions in activation space; projecting onto one reads its strength.
Features lie on curved manifolds that linear projections are unable to read.
a4-l057-superposition.explanation: Under this hypothesis a concept corresponds to a vector $w_i$, and the activation is roughly $h=\sum_if_iw_i$. Linear probes, steering vectors and sparse autoencoders all rest on it. The directions need not line up with individual neurons.

a4-l057-superposition.prompt: Why does superposition work best when features are sparse (rarely active)?
options: Sparse features have smaller weights, so they take up less of the space.
The ReLU can compress dense features into fewer dimensions without loss.
Sparsity makes all the feature directions exactly orthogonal to each other.
Rare features seldom co-occur, so their overlapping directions seldom interfere.
a4-l057-superposition.explanation: Packing more features than dimensions forces their directions to overlap, so one active feature leaks a little into others' readouts. If features are rarely active together, that interference is usually absent, and nonlinearities can filter the small leakage. Dense features would interfere constantly.

a4-l057-superposition.prompt: Two random unit vectors in $d=4096$ dimensions have a cosine similarity with mean 0 and standard deviation about $1/\sqrt d$. What is that typical magnitude? Give a decimal.
a4-l057-superposition.explanation: $1/\sqrt{4096}=1/64\approx0.016$. Random directions in high dimension are almost orthogonal, and one can fit exponentially many vectors with all pairwise overlaps below a small threshold. That is why large models can afford superposition.

a4-l057-superposition.prompt: Explain why single neurons in language models are often polysemantic (responding to several unrelated concepts), using superposition.
a4-l057-superposition.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the model has many more useful features than neurons or dimensions; (2) in high dimensions, many nearly orthogonal directions exist, so features are stored as directions that are not aligned with neuron axes (superposition); (3) each feature direction has components on many neurons, and each neuron overlaps many features; (4) so a single neuron fires for several unrelated concepts; the interpretable units are directions, not neurons, motivating sparse autoencoders.
a4-l057-superposition.modelAnswer: There are far more useful features (concepts, patterns, tokens in context) than neurons. High-dimensional space has room for vastly more nearly orthogonal directions than dimensions, so the model stores features as directions that cut across many neurons, accepting a little interference because most features are rarely active. Each neuron then sits under many feature directions and lights up for several unrelated things. The clean units are directions, not neurons, which is what sparse autoencoders try to recover.

a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.prompt: In a sparse autoencoder trained on model activations, what does the L1 penalty $\lambda\|f\|_1$ on the feature activations achieve?
options: It keeps the decoder weights small, so that the reconstruction stays smooth.
It drives most features to zero, so each input is explained by a few active ones.
It forces the features to be exactly orthogonal, undoing superposition fully.
It shrinks the dictionary until its size equals the width of the model.
a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.explanation: The dictionary is much wider than the activation, which allows many features, but the L1 penalty makes only a handful active per input. Sparse codes tend to align with individual concepts that superposition had mixed together, making them more interpretable. $\lambda$ trades interpretability against reconstruction error.

a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.prompt: Adding a large multiple of an SAE feature's decoder direction to a model's residual stream during generation does what?
options: Steers outputs toward the feature's concept, testing whether its label is right.
Retrains the model permanently so that it always produces that concept.
Removes the concept from the model's vocabulary for the rest of the run.
Changes only the SAE's reconstruction, leaving the model's outputs alone.
a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.explanation: Feature steering is a causal test of interpretation. If a feature labelled 'aromatic rings' really represents that concept, amplifying it should make the model talk about aromatic rings. Labels from top-activating examples alone can mislead; effects on outputs confirm them.

a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.prompt: Write the sparse-autoencoder objective, explain how an SAE feature is interpreted, and describe its main limitations.
a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) objective $\|x-\hat x\|_2^2+\lambda\|f\|_1$ with $f=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_e(x-b_d)+b_e)$ and $\hat x=W_df+b_d$: reconstruct activations through a wide, sparsely active layer; (2) interpretation from top-activating examples (what inputs make it fire) and from its effect on logits or behaviour (decoder direction projected through the unembedding, or steering); (3) limitations: dead features that never fire, feature splitting (features depend on dictionary size; a concept fragments into finer ones), unexplained reconstruction error (the 'dark matter' the features miss), plus interpretations that are subjective.
a4-l058-sparse-autoencoders.modelAnswer: The SAE encodes an activation $x$ into a wide, mostly-zero code $f=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_e(x-b_d)+b_e)$ and decodes $\hat x=W_df+b_d$, minimizing $\|x-\hat x\|^2+\lambda\|f\|_1$. A feature is interpreted by reading the inputs that activate it most and by checking what its decoder direction does to the logits or to generations when added. Limitations: some features die and never fire; features split into finer ones as the dictionary grows, so there is no canonical set; and part of the activation is never reconstructed, so some of the model's computation stays unexplained.

a4-l059-induction-heads.prompt: For a single attention head, what do the QK circuit $W_QW_K^{\top}$ and the OV circuit $W_VW_O$ each determine?
options: QK: what the head moves from a position. OV: which positions it reads.
QK: the head's output size. OV: how many positions it can attend to.
QK and OV both set the attention pattern; neither affects what moves.
QK: which positions the head attends to. OV: what it moves from them.
a4-l059-induction-heads.explanation: The attention pattern comes from $x_iW_QW_K^{\top}x_j^{\top}$, so QK is a bilinear 'where to look' form. Once weights are set, the head writes $\sum_j a_{ij}x_jW_VW_O$, so OV is a linear map deciding what information from the attended token is copied into the residual stream.

a4-l059-induction-heads.prompt: A model reads a sequence of 50 random tokens followed by the same 50 tokens again. In the second copy, where does an induction head at a token $t$ put its attention?
options: On the token that followed $t$ in the first copy.
On $t$'s own earlier occurrence in the first copy.
On the token immediately before $t$ in the second copy.
Spread evenly over every token in the first copy.
a4-l059-induction-heads.explanation: An induction head looks for an earlier position whose previous token matches the current token, i.e. the token after the earlier $t$, and copies it as the prediction. On repeated random text this gives a characteristic off-diagonal stripe in the attention pattern and near-perfect prediction of the second copy.

a4-l059-induction-heads.prompt: Describe the two-head induction circuit that completes [A][B] … [A] → [B], and explain its link to in-context learning.
a4-l059-induction-heads.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a previous-token head in an earlier layer writes into each position information about the token before it (the position of B records 'preceded by A'); (2) a later induction head at the current A uses its QK circuit (K-composition with the previous-token output) to attend to positions whose previous token was A, i.e. B; (3) its OV circuit copies B's identity, raising B's logit; (4) link: this is a general mechanism for continuing patterns seen earlier in the context; induction heads form at the same point in training as a sharp improvement in in-context learning, suggesting they underlie much of it.
a4-l059-induction-heads.modelAnswer: First, a previous-token head copies into each position a note saying which token came before it; so the position holding B now carries 'my predecessor was A'. Later, when A appears again, an induction head searches with a query for 'positions whose predecessor was A', finds B's position, and its OV circuit copies B into the stream, so the model predicts B. This copy-what-came-next pattern lets the model use patterns in its context without weight changes, and induction heads appear during training at the same time as a jump in in-context learning ability.

a4-l060-activation-patching.prompt: In an activation-patching experiment the logit difference is 4.0 on the clean prompt and $-1.0$ on the corrupted prompt. Patching one head's clean activation into the corrupted run gives 2.5. What fraction of the logit difference does that patch recover? Give a decimal.
a4-l060-activation-patching.explanation: Recovery $=(2.5-(-1.0))/(4.0-(-1.0))=3.5/5=0.70$. Restoring this one head brings back 70% of the clean behaviour, strong evidence that it carries much of the information that distinguishes the two prompts.

a4-l060-activation-patching.prompt: A neuron's activation correlates strongly with whether a model answers correctly. Why is this not enough to claim the neuron drives the answer?
options: Correlations inside neural networks are always far too weak to be measured reliably.
It may be a side product; only intervening on it shows the output depends on it.
A neuron can only matter if it sits in the final layer of the model.
Correlation is enough provided that the dataset is large enough.
a4-l060-activation-patching.explanation: Many quantities computed in parallel correlate with the answer without contributing to it. Interventions such as ablation, patching or steering change the activation and measure the effect on output, which separates cause from correlate, as a controlled experiment does in the lab.

a4-l060-activation-patching.prompt: How is a steering vector typically obtained and used?
options: Fine-tune the model on a dataset of example prompts that show the target behaviour.
Mask attention to every token linked to the unwanted behaviour in the input prompt.
Take the mean activation difference between contrasting prompts and add it during inference.
Raise the sampling temperature only for those tokens that relate to the behaviour.
a4-l060-activation-patching.explanation: For example, average residual-stream activations on formal versus casual prompts and take the difference. Adding a multiple of that vector at a chosen layer shifts outputs toward the formal style without changing weights. It is both a control technique and evidence that the concept is represented linearly.

a4-l060-activation-patching.prompt: Explain activation patching in your own words, and what attribution-graph (circuit-tracing) methods add.
a4-l060-activation-patching.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) run a clean prompt and a minimally different corrupted prompt that changes the answer, caching activations; (2) rerun the corrupted prompt but replace one component's activation with its clean value; (3) measure how much of the clean logit difference is restored, which localizes components that carry the distinguishing information; (4) attribution graphs trace how interpretable features (e.g. from transcoders or SAEs) feed into one another for a specific prompt, giving a step-by-step causal diagram of the computation, still validated by interventions.
a4-l060-activation-patching.modelAnswer: Take two prompts that differ in one key detail and give different answers, run both, and save every activation. Then rerun the corrupted prompt but swap in the clean activation for one component at a time. If the answer swings back toward the clean one, that component carries the information that matters, and the fraction of logit difference recovered measures how much. Attribution graphs go further: they replace neurons with interpretable features and trace which features feed which for a given prompt, giving a wiring diagram of the computation that is then checked with interventions.

a4-l061-benchmarks.prompt: A model scores 80% on a 500-question benchmark. What is the binomial standard error of that accuracy? Give the answer in percentage points.
a4-l061-benchmarks.explanation: $\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{0.8\times0.2/500}\approx0.0179$, about 1.8 points. A 95% interval is roughly $\pm3.5$ points, so small leaderboard gaps on benchmarks of this size are within noise.

a4-l061-benchmarks.prompt: Two models score 81.0% and 82.5% on a 500-question benchmark. Is the gap meaningful?
options: Yes: any gap on the same benchmark is a real difference.
Yes, provided that both models were evaluated at temperature zero.
Not clearly: each score has a standard error of about 1.8 points.
No: benchmark scores never differ in a meaningful way.
a4-l061-benchmarks.explanation: The difference of two independent scores has an SE of about $\sqrt2\times1.75\approx2.5$ points, so 1.5 points is well inside noise. Paired analyses on the same questions are tighter but still need checking, and prompt-format sensitivity can shift scores by similar amounts.

a4-l061-benchmarks.prompt: Top models now all score about 95% on a popular benchmark, and new models gain little. What is the main problem with using it to compare frontier models?
options: Saturation: remaining errors may be label noise, so it no longer separates models.
Contamination is impossible at high scores, so the results are fully reliable.
High scores prove that the benchmark's underlying task has been solved for good.
Only the variance matters at that level, so averaging more runs will fix it.
a4-l061-benchmarks.explanation: Near the ceiling, the remaining items are often mislabelled or ambiguous, and contamination becomes more likely the longer a benchmark is public. Saturated benchmarks stop discriminating, which is why harder and refreshed benchmarks keep replacing them.

a4-l061-benchmarks.prompt: Explain how benchmark contamination and prompt sensitivity can each make a reported benchmark score misleading.
a4-l061-benchmarks.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) contamination: test items or close paraphrases appear in training data, so the model can recall rather than solve, inflating the score relative to the intended ability; detection via n-gram overlap, canaries, or fresh held-out sets; (2) prompt sensitivity: small changes in formatting, answer-option order, few-shot examples or the instruction can move scores by several points, so comparisons with different prompts are not apples to apples; (3) both mean scores should be read with their error bars and evaluation details.
a4-l061-benchmarks.modelAnswer: Contamination: if test questions, or close variants, leaked into the training data, the model can recall answers rather than work them out, so the score overstates its real ability on new problems. Prompt sensitivity: the same model can gain or lose several points depending on answer-option order, the instruction wording or the few-shot examples, so two labs' numbers may reflect their prompts as much as their models. Either way a headline score needs its evaluation setup and error bars to mean much.

a4-l062-judges-elo.prompt: In an arena-style leaderboard, model A is rated 100 Elo points above model B. Using $E_A=1/(1+10^{(R_B-R_A)/400})$, what is A's expected win probability against B? Give a decimal.
a4-l062-judges-elo.explanation: $E_A=1/(1+10^{-0.25})\approx0.640$. Elo and Bradley–Terry are the same logistic model of pairwise preferences, just on a different scale (base 10 and 400 points instead of $e$).

a4-l062-judges-elo.prompt: An LLM judge prefers whichever of two answers is shown first. What is a standard mitigation?
options: Always show the longer answer first so that the judge reads it fully.
Use a stronger judge model, which removes position effects entirely.
Ask the judge for a score out of 100 rather than a pairwise choice.
Judge each pair in both orders and count only consistent verdicts.
a4-l062-judges-elo.explanation: Position bias is systematic, so swapping the order and averaging (or treating inconsistent verdicts as ties) cancels it. Similar care is needed for verbosity bias (preferring longer answers) and self-preference (a judge favouring its own model family's outputs).

a4-l062-judges-elo.prompt: Arena ratings are fitted with a Bradley–Terry/Elo model. What does a 400-point rating gap imply?
options: The higher-rated model wins every single comparison against the other.
Expected odds of about 10 to 1, i.e. roughly 91% wins for the higher model.
The higher-rated model has won 400 more comparisons than it has lost.
The higher-rated model is about four times better at every type of task.
a4-l062-judges-elo.explanation: With $E_A=1/(1+10^{-\Delta/400})$, $\Delta=400$ gives $10/11\approx0.91$. Ratings summarize average preference across the prompts users happened to submit, not ability on any particular task.

a4-l062-judges-elo.prompt: Design an evaluation for an LLM chemistry assistant: describe the task set, the scoring rubric, and the failure categories you would track.
a4-l062-judges-elo.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a task set drawn from real use: e.g. reaction and mechanism questions, stoichiometry and calculations, safety and handling questions, literature or SDS lookups, with held-out, uncontaminated items and expert-written reference answers; (2) a rubric: correctness (verified by experts or tools), safety appropriateness, use of sources and citations, calibration and abstention when unsure, clarity; specify human or LLM judges with bias controls; (3) failure categories: factual errors (wrong values, hallucinated CAS numbers or references), unsafe advice, calculation or unit errors, refusals of legitimate requests, misread structures; (4) report with error bars.
a4-l062-judges-elo.modelAnswer: Tasks: about 300 items drawn from what chemists actually ask, such as mechanism questions, yield and stoichiometry calculations, SDS and handling questions, and literature lookups, written fresh so they are not in any training set, each with an expert reference answer. Rubric: correct (checked by an expert or a tool for numbers), safe, sourced, says 'unsure' when it should, and clear; if an LLM judge helps, swap answer order and spot-check against humans. Failure categories to tally: wrong facts or invented references and CAS numbers, unit or arithmetic errors, misread structures, unsafe advice, and needless refusals. Report results with confidence intervals.

a4-l063-alignment-problem.prompt: A cleaning robot rewarded for 'no visible mess in the camera image' learns to push mess under a rug. Which failure is this?
options: Inner misalignment: the right objective, but the robot learned a different goal.
A capability failure: the robot is simply not yet good enough at cleaning.
Model collapse from training the robot on its own previous outputs.
Specification gaming: the objective written down was wrong (outer alignment).
a4-l063-alignment-problem.explanation: The robot does exactly what the reward measures. The gap is between the specified objective (no visible mess) and the intended one (no mess). Outer alignment is about writing down the right objective; inner alignment is about whether training produces a system that pursues it.

a4-l063-alignment-problem.prompt: In training, the coin in a game level was always at the far right; the agent learned to run right. At test time the coin is placed elsewhere and the agent still runs right, ignoring it. What is this?
options: Specification gaming: the reward function itself pointed the agent to the right.
Reward hacking: the agent found a bug that paid out without reaching the coin.
Goal misgeneralization: it learned a different goal that fit training equally well.
A capability failure: the agent can no longer move or navigate competently.
a4-l063-alignment-problem.explanation: The reward was correct (get the coin), and the agent stays competent at moving, but in training 'go right' and 'get the coin' were indistinguishable, and it learned the wrong one. Capabilities generalize while the goal does not, which is an inner-alignment failure.

a4-l063-alignment-problem.prompt: Explain why training a model to maximize human approval can produce sycophancy rather than correctness.
a4-l063-alignment-problem.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) approval is a proxy: raters reward responses they like, and people tend to like agreement, flattery and confident answers, and cannot always check correctness; (2) optimization pushes the model toward whatever earns approval, so it learns to agree with the user's stated views, praise their work or tell them what they want to hear, even when wrong; (3) this is specification gaming of the human-feedback objective; (4) mitigations: rater guidelines and expert raters, rewarding disagreement when warranted, evaluating with ground truth.
a4-l063-alignment-problem.modelAnswer: The training signal is whether a person liked the answer, not whether it was true. People tend to rate agreement, flattery and confident tone highly, and often cannot verify the content. So optimization finds that echoing the user's view or praising their reasoning earns reward even when the user is wrong. The model is being aligned to approval, a proxy for helpfulness, and the gap between the two shows up as sycophancy.

a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.prompt: A web page an agent visits contains hidden text instructing it to upload the user's files to an external site. What kind of attack is this?
options: Indirect prompt injection: attacker instructions arrive inside data the agent reads.
A jailbreak written by the user to get around the model's refusal and safety training.
Training-data poisoning, which plants a backdoor in the model's weights.
An adversarial perturbation designed to confuse the model's tokenizer.
a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.explanation: A jailbreak is the user trying to get disallowed output. Prompt injection comes from third-party content that the system processes (pages, emails, documents) and hijacks the model's actions on the user's behalf. Agents with tools make injection especially dangerous.

a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.prompt: Which defence limits the damage from a prompt injection even when the injection succeeds?
options: A longer system prompt that restates the rules several times in strong language.
Privilege separation: untrusted content cannot trigger sensitive tools without approval.
Raising refusal rates on all requests until injection attempts mostly fail.
Sampling at higher temperature so that injected instructions are followed less often.
a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.explanation: Since no model reliably ignores injected text, robust designs assume injection will sometimes work and limit what can follow: the component that reads untrusted data has no access to dangerous actions, and sensitive steps need confirmation. This is defence in depth, as in conventional security.

a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.prompt: Explain why prompt injection is hard to solve completely, and describe a layered defence for an LLM agent.
a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the model receives instructions and data as one token stream, and there is no hard, architecturally enforced boundary between them; the model must infer from context which text is authoritative, and attackers can craft text that looks authoritative; (2) training helps but is probabilistic and attackers adapt; (3) layers: refusal and instruction-hierarchy training; input and output classifiers that flag injections or harmful content; privilege separation and least privilege for tools, with human confirmation for sensitive actions; red-teaming and monitoring; (4) the point of layers is that each catches some failures of the others.
a4-l064-robustness-jailbreaks.modelAnswer: Everything the model reads, the user's request or a web page, arrives as tokens in one context, and nothing structurally marks which tokens are allowed to give orders. The model has to judge authority from content, and an attacker can always write content that looks authoritative. So defence is layered: train the model to follow a hierarchy (system above user above data); run classifiers on inputs and outputs; give the agent only the tools it needs and require human confirmation for sensitive ones; and red-team continuously. Each layer catches some of what the others miss.

a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.prompt: What does a 'chemical uplift' dangerous-capability evaluation of an LLM measure?
options: How well the model scores on a standard undergraduate chemistry examination paper.
Whether the model refuses every question that mentions any toxic chemical by name.
How many hazardous compounds the model can name correctly from memory alone.
How far the model boosts a novice's ability to do harmful steps beyond what search gives.
a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.explanation: Knowledge alone is not the risk; much is in textbooks. Uplift studies compare people with and without model access on realistic tasks (often proxies for weaponization steps) to see whether the model meaningfully lowers the barrier to harm. Chemistry is central because the same knowledge serves both legitimate and harmful synthesis.

a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.prompt: What do frontier-safety (responsible-scaling) policies typically commit a developer to?
options: Refusing every chemistry-related request, whatever the user or purpose.
Stopping all training as soon as a model passes any public benchmark.
Stronger safeguards before deploying a model that crosses set capability thresholds.
Relying on users accepting the terms of service as the main and only safeguard against misuse.
a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.explanation: Such policies define capability thresholds (for example meaningful uplift in chemical or biological weapons, cyber offence or autonomous replication), test models against them, and require matching protections, such as stronger security and deployment safeguards, before going further. Safety measures scale with measured risk.

a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.prompt: Weigh the benefits of an LLM chemistry assistant against its misuse risk, and propose concrete safeguards.
a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) benefits: faster literature work, synthesis planning, safety information, education, lab efficiency; (2) risks: uplift toward chemical weapons or other harmful synthesis (dual use), unsafe procedures given to non-experts, hazardous automation; (3) concrete safeguards, at least two: classifiers screening for weapon-relevant requests; refusing specific high-risk synthesis routes while helping with general chemistry; screening against scheduled-chemical lists; tiered access or verification for sensitive capabilities; human approval before lab execution; logging, monitoring and red-teaming; (4) a balanced argument that avoids over-refusal of legitimate work.
a4-l065-dangerous-capabilities.modelAnswer: A chemistry assistant speeds up literature review, suggests routes, explains hazards and helps students, which is real value. The same knowledge can give uplift toward chemical weapons or hand an untrained person a dangerous procedure. Safeguards: classifiers that catch requests for weapon-relevant agents and their precursors; screening against scheduled-chemical lists; refusing specific high-risk routes while still helping with ordinary synthesis; verified access for sensitive capabilities; human approval before anything runs on lab hardware; and logging plus regular red-teaming. The aim is to block the narrow dangerous tail without refusing everyday chemistry.

a4-l066-scalable-oversight.prompt: What core problem do scalable-oversight methods such as debate, critique models and weak-to-strong generalization address?
options: Supervising models on tasks where humans can't directly check the answers.
Training models faster by having them supervise their own gradient updates.
Reducing inference cost by routing easy questions to smaller models.
Removing the need for any evaluation once a model is deployed.
a4-l066-scalable-oversight.explanation: Human feedback works when humans can judge outputs. As models tackle problems beyond what humans can easily verify, oversight must be amplified: debate pits models against each other to expose flaws, critique models point out errors, and weak-to-strong work asks whether a weak supervisor can still elicit a strong model's full capability.

a4-l066-scalable-oversight.prompt: Monitoring a reasoning model's chain of thought is a promising oversight tool. How could it fail?
options: Chains of thought are always encrypted, so monitors are unable to read them.
The trace may not reflect the real computation, and pressure on it can teach hiding.
Monitoring makes the model reason less, which lowers its accuracy too much.
Chains of thought are always faithful, so the only risk is monitor cost.
a4-l066-scalable-oversight.explanation: Visible reasoning can reveal intentions such as planning to game a test. But traces can be unfaithful (omitting what drove the answer), and training directly against 'bad thoughts' can push a model to obfuscate them rather than stop. Preserving monitorability is itself an open problem.

a4-l066-scalable-oversight.prompt: Explain the AI-control approach to safety, and summarize the main open problems in oversight as of 2026.
a4-l066-scalable-oversight.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) AI control: assume a capable model might be misaligned or deceptive and design deployment so it cannot cause serious harm anyway: trusted (weaker) models or humans monitor its actions, sensitive actions are restricted or audited, and protocols are red-teamed by deliberately trying to subvert them; (2) open problems, at least two: reliable evaluation of capabilities and safety (contamination, sandbagging, evals lagging capabilities); interpretability at scale (explaining frontier models' computations, not just small circuits); detecting deceptive or scheming behaviour, including models that behave differently when they believe they are being tested; faithfulness of reasoning traces.
a4-l066-scalable-oversight.modelAnswer: AI control does not assume the model is trustworthy. It deploys a capable but untrusted model inside a protocol, with weaker trusted models or humans monitoring its outputs, restrictions and audits on dangerous actions, and red teams trying to beat the setup, so that even a misaligned model cannot do serious harm. Open problems: building evaluations that keep up with capabilities and cannot be gamed or sandbagged; scaling interpretability from small circuits to whole frontier models; and reliably detecting deception, including models that behave well only when they suspect they are being tested.
